content.title: About
content.content: Stew meat is a cut of beef, usually taken from the shoulder, neck, or round, cut into small cubes. It has a rich beefy flavor, moderate fat content, and holds its shape well during long cooking, making it perfect for stews, soups, and slow‑cooked dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stew meat is often sold pre‑cubed, saving prep time.
Shoulder cuts contain connective tissue that turns into gelatin during slow cooking, thickening the sauce.
Different regions use different names: in the US it’s called "stew meat," while in Russia it’s referred to as "тушеное мясо."
Best cooked at low temperatures (90‑120 °C) for 2‑4 hours.
When stored properly, it stays fresh in the fridge for up to 3 days and up to 6 months in the freezer.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc aids immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Provides creatine
items.content: Creatine contributes to increased muscular energy, especially during intense exercise.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake may raise blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked beef can harbor pathogens such as E. coli and salmonella.

items.title: Rare beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: High purine levels can exacerbate gout symptoms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: For best results, sear the cubes until browned, then simmer in broth or sauce for 2‑4 hours. Use in beef stews, chili, pasta sauces, or as a filling for pies and empanadas.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a low‑air‑permeable bag for up to 6 months. Thaw in the refrigerator before cooking.

coffee-latte-with-non-dairy-milk-flavore.title: Coffee Latte with Non‑Dairy Milk and Flavor

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee latte with non‑dairy milk is a beverage made from espresso combined with steamed, frothed plant‑based milk (soy, oat, almond, coconut, etc.) and flavored with a syrup (vanilla, caramel, hazelnut, etc.). It blends the boldness of coffee with the creamy texture of milk and a pleasant aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Latte originates from Italy, where the word “latte” simply means “milk”.
Plant‑based milks allow lactose‑intolerant consumers to enjoy latte without discomfort.
Flavored syrups often use natural extracts but may contain added sugars.
Vegan lattes became a mainstream offering in coffee shops worldwide in the early 2010s.
The combination of caffeine and plant fats can slow the release of energy, providing a longer‑lasting boost.

items.title: Caffeine’s alertness boost
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving focus and reducing fatigue.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Plant milks contain no lactose, making the drink safe for those with lactase deficiency.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Many plant milks are fortified with calcium, vitamin D and B12, supporting bone health and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Some plant milks (e.g., oat) provide soluble fiber that promotes a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: In some individuals caffeine can cause anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Sugar content in syrups
items.content: Flavored syrups often add significant sugar, which may contribute to weight gain and dental issues.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: Soy, almond, or coconut milks can trigger allergic reactions in susceptible people.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of stimulants and reduce the efficacy of sedatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the latte hot or iced, adding the desired flavored syrup. Top with a sprinkle of cinnamon, cocoa powder, or vegan whipped cream. Prepare espresso, then pour steamed plant‑based milk in a 1:3 ratio and stir in syrup to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The prepared drink is best enjoyed immediately. If you need to store it, keep it in a sealed container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Store unopened plant milk according to the manufacturer’s instructions, usually refrigerated after opening.

content.title: About
content.content: Flavored rice mixture (3840) is a ready‑to‑cook blend of selected rice, spices, dried vegetables and aromatic herbs. The mix is designed for quick preparation of a tasty side dish without the need to add separate seasonings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend contains medium‑ and long‑grain rice that holds its shape during cooking.
Spices such as turmeric, paprika, garlic and onion give the dish a golden colour and rich aroma.
Dried vegetables (carrot, peas, corn) add texture and boost nutritional value.
No additional soy sauce or ready sauces are required – everything is pre‑balanced.
One package yields 3‑4 servings, convenient for family meals.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides a slow‑release energy source, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and B6 vitamins from the rice and spices support normal metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Turmeric and paprika supply curcumin and carotenoids, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dried vegetables and spices stimulate gastric juice production, improving nutrient absorption.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The mixture is virtually fat‑free, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to turmeric, paprika or dried vegetables.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: While no salt is added, certain spices may contribute a small amount of sodium.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Processing may involve auxiliary ingredients containing gluten; check the label if you have celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse the rice, then add 2‑2.5 cups of water and the mixture, bring to a boil. Reduce heat, cover, and simmer 15‑20 minutes until tender. Finish with fresh herbs if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from moisture and direct sunlight. After opening, transfer any remaining mixture to an airtight container.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-and-m.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce and Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with cream sauce and meat is a home recipe that combines nutritious whole‑grain noodles, a velvety cream sauce, and flavorful meat. The dish is rich in protein, fiber, and healthy fats, offering a satisfying taste and lasting fullness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta retains the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than traditional white pasta.
Cream sauce is often made from heavy cream and broth, giving the dish a silky texture.
Meat is usually beef or pork, but chicken or turkey can be used for a lighter version.
Pasta is traditionally cooked al dente to preserve a slight bite and lower the glycemic index.
A homemade recipe lets you control salt and fat levels, creating a healthier meal.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat and whole‑grain pasta provide a complete set of amino acids that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour keeps the bran, which aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Cream and a modest amount of oil supply monounsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole grains are abundant in B1, B2, B3, and B6 vitamins that help energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, zinc, and magnesium, important for immunity and nerve function.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and meat make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cream contains saturated fat, which can raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta contains gluten and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Using store‑bought broth can increase sodium; opt for low‑salt versions to keep the dish heart‑friendly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the cream sauce and sautéed meat pieces. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, or vegetables such as broccoli or spinach for added flavor and nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. The cream sauce may separate; gently reheat and stir before serving. The dish can be frozen, though the pasta texture may change slightly after thawing.

content.title: About
content.content: Pot pie, no meat is a baked pie with a flaky crust and a filling of vegetables, legumes and aromatic spices. It is suitable for vegetarians and anyone looking for a lighter alternative to traditional meat pies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Classic American pot pie is usually made with chicken, but the vegetarian version keeps the creamy sauce.
Mushrooms are often used to mimic a "meaty" texture.
Legumes such as peas or chickpeas add protein and make the dish more filling.
The crust can be made with whole‑grain flour, increasing fiber content.
Meat‑free pot pies are popular in colder months as a comforting warm meal.

items.title: Rich in vegetables
items.content: The vegetable mix (carrot, celery, onion) provides vitamins A, C and K as well as antioxidants.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Legumes contribute complete plant protein, beneficial for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Fiber from vegetables and whole‑grain crust supports digestion and satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Absence of meat reduces saturated fat, which is favorable for heart health.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Mushrooms and legumes are good sources of non‑heme iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to peas, chickpeas or other legumes used in the filling.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces can be salty; people monitoring sodium should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Gluten in crust
items.content: Traditional crust contains wheat; a gluten‑free alternative is needed for celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The pie can be calorie‑dense due to butter‑based sauce and crust; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat the pie in the oven or microwave until the crust is golden. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs or a light yogurt sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked pie in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for up to 2 months. Ensure it is thoroughly heated before consumption.
